title: Academic Task 1 - Comparing and contrasting graphs and tables
subtitle: Lexical Resource and Grammatical Accuracy
summary: Paraphrase the question instead of copying it, choose the right tense for each change, and write numbers, plurals and prepositions accurately.

lesson.heading: Repetition costs you Lexical Resource
lesson.text: **Lexical Resource** assesses the accuracy and **range** of your vocabulary. Repeating your own words - or the words of the question - is the quickest way to keep that score down. Synonyms are the cheapest fix.

examples.text: a sharp **decrease** - a sharp **reduction**
the figures **fell** - the figures **dropped**
numbers will **increase** - numbers will **rise**
numbers will **remain** the same - numbers will **stay** the same
the charts **show** - the charts **indicate**
the **data** in the table - the **information** in the table

lesson.heading: Never copy the question's introductory sentence
lesson.text: Your opening statement must be in **your own words**. Two techniques do all the work: use a synonym, and change the **form** of a word - a verb into a noun, a noun into a phrase.

examples.text: *The graph shows traffic growth in the Netherlands.*
examples.note: The graph **indicates the changes in the number of vehicles on the road** in the Netherlands.

examples.text: *The bar chart shows the sporting preferences of 100 adults, boys and girls.*
examples.note: The bar chart tells us the **different sports preferred by a group of people of a range of ages**.

examples.text: *The graphs show the number of students that have attended the college and their nationalities.*
examples.note: From the graphs we can see **how many** students **have taken courses at** the college and **the countries they come from**.

examples.text: *The two pie charts show the average household expenditure in the US.*
examples.note: The pie charts reveal **how much people spent** in the US in 1900 and in 2000.

lesson.note: *Shows* becomes *indicates*, *tells us*, *reveals*, *we can see*. Four questions, four different verbs.

lesson.heading: Tense follows the time in the figure
rows: *The figures for UK households **remained** fairly steady between 2000 and 2002.*
*Wealth **has risen** from £4,500 billion to just under £7,000 billion.*
*this trend **did not last** long and **began to worsen** again a year later*
*It **is predicted that** the numbers will begin to increase from 2025.*
lesson.note: Grammatical Range and Accuracy is a separate criterion. A description in one tense throughout will not score well even if every fact is right.

lesson.heading: Three things a sentence can do

left.label: Describe one sector
examples: *The figures for UK households remained fairly steady between 2000 and 2002.*
*From 2005 to 2007 the rest of the country experienced continued growth.*

right.label: Compare or contrast two
examples: *Both the government and household wealth showed figures that gradually increased.* (similarity)
*While both dropped significantly in 2008, the government's net worth fell so much that it went into negative figures.* (contrast)
*At the same time that the wealth of households grew, the wealth of businesses declined.* (contrast)

lesson.note: *Both*, *similar*, *at the same time* signal similarity; *while*, *although*, *whereas*, *the opposite trend* signal contrast.

lesson.heading: Numbers: figures or words?
lesson.text: Write **exact amounts, percentages and years** as numerals. Write **fractions and approximate quantities** as words. Mixing the two carelessly reads as an error.

examples.text: Numerals: *£7000 billion*, *5% to 10%*, *2002 to 2004*
Words: *six of the ten years*, *just under a third*
*½ of the people* - **half** of the people
*They reduced the budget by $1m* - by **one million dollars**
*¼ of those* - **a quarter** of those
*rose by 3½ billion* - by **three and a half billion**

lesson.heading: The two mistakes that cost the most
lesson.text: Candidates lose marks on the same two points again and again: the final **-s**, and the **preposition**.

examples.text: *There were approximately three **hundred** **thousand** **cars** on the roads in 1970.*
examples.note: *hundred* and *thousand* stay singular after a number; *cars* takes the -s.

examples.text: ***Millions** of people travel by plane every year.*
*four **hundred** **beds** were manufactured*
The increase **in** car use; the number **of** students; 70% **of** women
The figures **for** train and bicycle use; increased **from** 35% **to** over 60%

lesson.text: When you practise, read your answer aloud. If your sentences all sound the same, the problem is structure, not vocabulary - and Grammatical Range is marked on exactly that.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with a synonym that would avoid repeating it.
The question reads *The graph shows traffic growth in the Netherlands between 1960 and 2010.* Which opening sentence is best?
options: The graph shows traffic growth in the Netherlands between 1960 and 2010.
The graph indicates the changes in the number of vehicles on the road in the Netherlands from 1960 to 2010.
This is a graph about traffic.
The graph shows that traffic in the Netherlands grew a lot.
exercises.explanation: It replaces *shows* with *indicates* and turns *traffic growth* into *the changes in the number of vehicles on the road* - synonym plus a change of word form.

exercises.prompt: *The figures for UK households ___ fairly steady between 2000 and 2002.* (remain)
exercises.explanation: A closed period with both dates given takes the past simple.

exercises.prompt: Does each sentence describe one sector, or compare two?

items.text: The figures for UK households remained fairly steady.
From 2005 to 2007 the rest of the country experienced continued growth.
Both the government and household wealth showed gradual increases.
While both dropped in 2008, the government's net worth went negative.
At the same time that household wealth grew, business wealth declined.

exercises.prompt: *There were approximately three hundred ___ cars on the roads in 1970.* (thousand)
exercises.explanation: *Hundred*, *thousand* and *million* stay singular directly after a number. *Millions of people* takes the -s because no number precedes it.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence writes its numbers the way IELTS expects?
options: ½ of the people who attended in 1961 had never attended a concert before.
Half of the people who attended in 1961 had never attended a concert before.
Half of the people who attended in nineteen sixty-one had never attended a concert before.
0.5 of the people who attended in 1961 had never attended a concert before.
exercises.explanation: Fractions and approximations go in words; exact years stay as numerals.

exercises.prompt: *The increase ___ car use was accompanied by a decline in the use of public transport.*
exercises.explanation: *An increase in* something; *the number of* something; *a percentage of* something. These collocations are worth learning as fixed pairs.

exercises.statement: Copying the question's own introductory sentence is safe, because it is guaranteed to be accurate.
exercises.explanation: Copied words do not count towards your own vocabulary range, and they may not count towards your word total either.

exercises.prompt: Build a sentence that contrasts two sectors.
exercises.answer: At the same time that household wealth grew, business wealth declined.
exercises.explanation: One clause for each sector, joined by a phrase that makes the contrast explicit - exactly what *make comparisons where relevant* asks for.

exercises.prompt: *The figures had increased ___ 35% ___ over 60% within five years.* Which pair of prepositions is correct?
exercises.explanation: *From X to Y* gives a starting and finishing value. Missing or wrong prepositions are one of the two most common number errors.
